title: How metrics systems work
summary: Series count, replication and query work decide the size of a metrics platform.

steps.title: One new label fills memory
steps.text: A latency metric has labels for service, route, region and status. Someone adds request_id. Suddenly almost every request creates a new series. The sample rate did not change much, but the series metadata and index did. In a metrics system, each distinct metric name and label set identifies a time series.

steps.title: The ingest and storage path
steps.text: Every label combination creates a series. Follow counted samples from the log into blocks and compaction, then repeat and shift a four-slice query.

steps.title: Worked example: cardinality and bytes
steps.text: Suppose 100 services each expose 20 routes in 3 regions with 5 status classes. If all combinations exist, one metric has 30,000 series. Sampling every 15 seconds gives 2,000 samples/s. At the catalog's roughly 1.5 compressed bytes/sample, 15 days hold about 3.89 GB of sample payload before replication, indexes and metadata. Multiplying by a million possible request ids can make the upper bound enormous, though actual cardinality depends on observed combinations. At an assumed 2 KB of active metadata per series, even 10 million active series need about 20 GB before samples. This example is not a simulated memory allocation.

steps.q: Samples/s stays fixed, but a new user-id label creates many short-lived series. Why can memory rise?
choices: Per-series metadata and churn grow independently of sample count
The same sample count must consume the same memory after compression
Only historical object storage grows; active memory depends solely on samples/s
steps.why: Samples and active-series state are separate costs. Churn also creates WAL and index work.

steps.q: Why does the bill rise when the sample count barely changes? Follow-up: which tenant limit do you add first?
checklist: Separate samples/s, active-series count and new-series rate
Calculate 20 GB for ten million series at assumed 2 KB each
Cap active series first, then churn, and expose rejection reasons
steps.model: I would look at active series and new-series rate as well as samples/s. A request id can turn reused series into short-lived ones, increasing metadata, index and WAL work. If active metadata is about 2 KB, ten million series already need about 20 GB before sample buffers. For this memory incident I would cap active series first, then bound new-series rate to control churn. I would return a rejection reason and show quota usage. Query scanned work needs separate limits. One universal requests/s limit cannot represent these costs.

steps.title: Do not let queries starve writes
steps.text: A query frontend splits long time ranges into bounded pieces and schedules them across workers. Each worker selects relevant blocks and series, then merges partial results. Cache historical results with tenant, authorization scope and full query semantics in the key. Immutable blocks do not guarantee immutable results: late data, deletions, lookback windows and query evaluation times can change them. Use a stable-data cutoff, invalidation or a bounded TTL. Fresh ranges need a short TTL or an explicit cutoff. Limit query concurrency, scanned bytes, range length, samples and wall time per tenant, independently of ingest limits. Limit active series, new-series rate and samples/s on writes. Fair queues let a small tenant make progress beside an expensive scan. Replication multiplies recent write work; object storage durability is a separate mechanism. Measure both query p99 and data freshness, since acknowledging buffered writes is not the same as making them queryable.

steps.q: One window has 10 requests averaging 10 ms; another has 90 averaging 100 ms. What is the combined mean?
choices: 55 ms, averaging the two window means
100 ms, using the larger window's mean for the whole period
91 ms, using total duration divided by total count
steps.why: (10 × 10 + 90 × 100) ÷ 100 = 91 ms. Keep sum and count when combining unequal windows.

steps.q: Why keep a durable recent-write log and object blocks? Follow-up: an ingester dies before its next flush.
checklist: Recover accepted samples not yet published in verified object blocks
State log fsync and host or zone loss guarantees at acknowledgement
Measure replay time and query visibility lag separately
steps.model: Blocks arrive after ingestion, so accepted samples still need a durable recovery source until upload is complete and verified. That can be replicated ingester WALs or a separate replicated ingest log. I would state whether acknowledgement waits for fsync and which host or zone failures it survives. A WAL append alone may only reach an operating-system buffer. Recovery replays from a checkpoint without duplicating logical samples. I would measure replay time and query visibility separately: a sample can be durable before an ingester has consumed it.

steps.q: A tenant stays under ingest quotas but launches 100 wide queries. Which control bounds its read-side work?
choices: A smaller active-series quota on newly ingested data alone
Per-tenant query concurrency, scanned work and execution deadlines
A global HTTP rate limit that counts each query as one request
steps.why: A wide query can cost far more than one write or lookup. Bound expensive work and schedule it fairly.

takeaway: Budget series, samples, replicated bytes and scanned query work separately.
